overview: The Warehouse Group is New Zealand's largest general merchandise retailer, operating three iconic NZ banners — The Warehouse (everyday low-price general merchandise, apparel, FMCG), Warehouse Stationery (office/school stationery and print & copy services), and Noel Leeming (electronics and appliances) — through a network of 216 physical stores plus online channels. The Group has struggled with a multi-year earnings downturn amid a weak NZ consumer environment, margin compression, and rising cost of doing business, and in FY2025 reported a group operating profit of just $1.3m and a net loss; a new CEO (Mark Stirton, formerly Group CFO) took over on 1 August 2025 and launched a cost-reset programme targeting cost of doing business below 31% of sales.

business_model.summary: Retail sales of owned/branded and third-party general merchandise, apparel, electronics/appliances and stationery through three banners, funded by supplier purchasing and store/online fulfilment; earns a retail gross margin (~32% Group) less cost of doing business (store rent, wages, distribution, corporate overhead). Revenue is transactional (no recurring subscription revenue) and highly seasonal (Christmas, back-to-school, EOFY). TheMarket.com online marketplace, launched 2019, was closed as a standalone front-end in 2024 after failing to meet expectations; its underlying engine now powers a Group Marketplace embedded within The Warehouse's own website/app rather than operating as a separate destination.
business_model.customer_type: B2C mass-market consumer, plus SME/education customers via Warehouse Stationery; online 6.7-7.0% of total sales (growing)
business_model.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand — no material international operations; imports sourced via 3 international sourcing offices (predominantly Asia) expose the Group to USD/FX and global freight costs

main_competitors: Amazon/Temu and other cross-border online retailers
PB Tech / JB Hi-Fi / Harvey Norman (electronics, competing with Noel Leeming)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest general merchandise/variety retailer in New Zealand by store footprint (84 Warehouse stores reaching 85% of NZ population within a 20-minute drive) and leading electronics retailer (Noel Leeming) and stationery/office retailer (Warehouse Stationery); however market position has eroded amid intensifying price competition and a weak consumer, with group operating margin collapsing to near breakeven (0-2%) over FY2023-FY2025

moat_factors.description: 216 stores nationwide with dense coverage gives convenience and reach that smaller/online-only competitors cannot easily replicate; The Warehouse alone reaches 85% of NZ population within 20 minutes

The Warehouse ('Red Sheds'), Noel Leeming and Warehouse Stationery are decades-old, widely recognised Kiwi retail brands, though brand strength has been diluted by inconsistent value proposition and margin-driven promotions
Private label products (e.g. Living & Co) represented 66% of sales with sustainable packaging characteristics in FY25, supporting margin and differentiation versus pure third-party resellers
Thin-margin, highly promotional NZ retail market limits pricing power; cost of doing business has been running above target (32.2% of sales vs <31% target), eroding any structural cost advantage

weaknesses: Persistent gross margin decline (33.6% to 32.2% in FY25) driven by an intentional 'everyday low price' reset and heavy clearance/promotional activity to compete on price
Group operating margin near breakeven (1.3% in FY25) leaves very little buffer against further sales or cost shocks
Heavy reliance on discretionary categories (apparel, home, big-ticket electronics) that are highly sensitive to NZ consumer confidence and cost-of-living pressure
Large, largely fixed lease cost base (~$709m lease liabilities, ~$620m long-term) from big-box/mall store network limits flexibility to right-size quickly
History of failed/scaled-back digital initiatives (TheMarket.com closure in 2024) raises questions about digital execution capability versus more digitally-native competitors

growth_drivers: Cost reset programme targeting cost of doing business below 31% of sales, including outsourcing/co-sourcing corporate functions to Tata Consultancy Services (~$110m targeted savings over two five-year contract terms) and a ~270 head-office role reduction (990 to ~720 roles) announced Feb 2026
New CEO Mark Stirton's turnaround strategy emphasising brand, culture and performance discipline, with a longer-term strategy to be articulated through FY26
Continued online sales growth (6.7% of sales in FY25, up to ~7.0% by Q1 FY26, 6.8% by Q3 FY26) via the Group Marketplace embedded in The Warehouse's own digital platform
Warehouse Stationery margin/growth outperformance (Print & Copy Centre services growing 7.2% at strong margins; FY26 H1 sales up 5.7%) as a relative bright spot within the portfolio

Store network optimisation — closing underperforming/uneconomic sites (e.g. The Warehouse Pakuranga, Tory Street; Noel Leeming Henderson Clearance Centre, Tokoroa) while selectively opening new stores (new standalone Warehouse Stationery, Wellington, Oct 2025) to improve sales density

RELEX AI-driven demand planning/forecasting rollout (live FY25) aimed at reducing stock-outs, improving inventory turns and reducing aged inventory (23.1% aged inventory in FY25 vs 19.9% FY24, a metric management is targeting to improve)
Improving units-sold trend (+4.6% FY25, +2.6% Q1 FY26) suggesting the everyday-low-price reset is driving volume, a precursor to margin recovery if cost discipline holds

business.description: Kmart, Briscoes, Bunnings/Mitre 10 and cross-border online players (Amazon, Temu) compete aggressively on price in a highly promotional NZ retail market, compressing margins across all three banners
Apparel, home and big-ticket electronics/whiteware categories (Noel Leeming) are highly sensitive to NZ consumer confidence, which management describes as remaining subdued
Cost reset targets (sub-31% CODB) and outsourcing to Tata depend on successful transition of corporate functions and realisation of projected savings without disrupting operations
A warmer winter in FY26 led to slower sell-through and increased clearance activity, illustrating ongoing sensitivity of margins to weather/seasonal demand and inventory management

Company has cycled through Interim CEO (John Journee) to new permanent CEO (Mark Stirton) within the past 18 months, alongside multiple other C-suite changes (new CFO, Chief Digital & Transformation Officer, Chief Legal Officer, Chief Merchandise Officer) — the FY25 annual report itself flags 'Leadership' as its top strategic risk

financial.description: ~$709m total lease liabilities (IFRS 16) versus ~$137m interest-bearing debt; lease interest (~$36.8m FY25) and principal repayments (~$104.9-141.7m/yr) represent a significant, largely fixed cash outflow regardless of sales performance
Board elected not to declare a dividend for FY25 given weak profitability; income-focused shareholders receive no current yield and resumption is contingent on a sustained earnings recovery

Group hedges NZD/USD exposure on import purchases (72.2% of forecast 12-month USD needs hedged at 1 Feb 2026 at ~0.59), but unhedged or rolling exposure to a weaker NZD raises landed cost of imported goods (majority of merchandise)

Shareholders' equity has nearly halved from $479m (FY18) to ~$300-310m (FY25/H1 FY26) as losses and dividends have eroded the capital base, though liquidity headroom remains (~$207-354m undrawn facilities)

regulatory.description: Employee expenses (largest single opex line, ~$527m FY25) are exposed to NZ minimum wage and general wage inflation running above CPI in some periods
Standard retail-sector compliance risk around product safety, consumer guarantees and advertising/pricing regulation
Moving ~270 head-office roles to Tata Consultancy Services offshore has drawn media and public attention to job losses, which carries reputational/political risk in NZ

macro.description: Chair and CEO both flag subdued consumer/business confidence and an economic slowdown as the dominant driver of FY25 underperformance, with no material improvement expected until at least end of calendar 2025/into 2026
High household debt levels in NZ mean mortgage rate changes materially affect discretionary spending capacity for The Warehouse Group's core customer base

H1 FY26 interim accounts flag the Iran conflict (US/Israel strikes, Feb 2026) as a subsequent event creating risk of higher global freight costs and shipping route disruption, with financial impact not yet quantifiable
Majority of merchandise is imported (largely from Asia); shipping costs, tariffs and commodity input costs for private-label goods directly affect landed cost of goods sold

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ general merchandise/discount retail is a large but low-growth, thin-margin, highly promotional market; industry-wide same-store sales have been roughly flat to slightly positive through FY25-FY26 as consumers remain cautious, with management not expecting a material shift in the economic outlook until confidence recovers
macro_factors.cyclicality: High — discretionary categories (apparel, electronics, big-ticket appliances) are consumer-discretionary and cyclical; stationery/back-to-school and FMCG-type staples within The Warehouse provide some counter-cyclical stability
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High indirect sensitivity via NZ mortgage rates and household disposable income; company itself carries floating-rate bank facilities plus fixed lease obligations

recent_developments.event: Mark Stirton (Group CFO since April 2024) formally stepped into the Group CEO role on 1 August 2025, succeeding Interim CEO John Journee, following a global search

FY2025 Annual Report released: Group sales $3.1bn (+1.6% reported, flat on 52-week same-store basis), gross margin down to 32.2% (from 33.6%), Operating Profit collapsed to $1.3m (from $28.9m FY24), reported net loss of $2.8m (vs $54.2m loss FY24); Board declared no FY25 dividend

Group announced a cost reset programme aimed at restoring profitability and bringing cost of doing business below 31% of sales, including an expanded co-sourcing partnership with Tata Consultancy Services for corporate/administrative functions

Confirmed cuts of 270 head-office roles (from ~990 to ~720), with total expected savings across two Tata outsourcing contract terms of approximately $110m over five years; several underperforming stores flagged for closure (Noel Leeming Henderson Clearance Centre and Tokoroa; The Warehouse Whangaparaoa, Johnsonville and Dunedin Central; Warehouse Stationery Te Awamutu)

H1 FY2026 interim results (26 weeks to 1 Feb 2026): sales $1,612.1m (+0.3%, like-for-like same-store +0.5%), operating profit up 37.7% to $26.9m (pre-IFRS16 group segment basis) / reported operating profit $47.0m including IFRS16 addback, net profit after tax $15.7m (vs $11.8m H1 FY25); Warehouse Stationery sales +5.7%, Noel Leeming sales -1.2%; no interim dividend declared; noted the Feb-2026 Iran conflict as a subsequent-event risk to freight costs

Q3 FY26 trading update (13 weeks to 3 May 2026): group sales down 1.4% to $700.8m, but gross margin up 50bps YoY and up 10bps YTD; foot traffic down 1.8% while average basket size up 2.7%; online sales up 5.4% to 6.8% of total sales
FY2026 full-year results (52 weeks to 2 August 2026) scheduled for release 30 September 2026

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2026 Interim Results / Q3 FY26 Trading Update (March-May 2026)

items.notes: CODB was 32.2% of sales in FY25 (improved 40bps from 32.6% FY24); management targets sub-31% via the cost reset programme and Tata co-sourcing, with a portion of labour savings ($3-4m) expected in FY26 and cumulative annualised savings of ~$17m by FY2031

items.target: ~$110m total over two 5-year contract terms (~$40m initial + ~$70m expanded)
items.vs_prior: raised (expanded scope announced Feb 2026 vs original Sept 2025 announcement)
items.notes: Covers technology, accounting, call centre and payroll functions; associated with ~270 head-office role reductions and $4.8m one-off restructuring/redundancy costs recognised in H1 FY26

items.target: no explicit FY26 quantum disclosed; historically curtailed
items.notes: FY25 capex was curtailed to $12.4m (out of $21.0m total project spend, down from $39.0m/$73.4m FY24); H1 FY26 capex of $6.6m suggests continued restrained spend for the full year

items.target: no interim or final dividend declared
items.notes: Board has not committed to a resumption date; contingent on sustained profitability improvement
Management has not issued explicit revenue or NPAT guidance; qualitative commentary points to 'improving profitability' and full FY26 results due 30 September 2026

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Mark Stirton has framed FY26 around three priorities — Brand, Culture and Performance — emphasising cost discipline, capital efficiency and 'measurable returns' rather than top-line growth targets. H1 FY26 results were characterised as 'improved profitability despite tough conditions,' with management citing disciplined cost control and improved working capital (lower inventory) as drivers. The Board and CEO have both cautioned that NZ economic recovery and consumer spending remain uncertain, and a longer-term strategic plan is expected to be articulated later in FY26/FY27.

bull_case: New CEO-led cost reset programme (Tata outsourcing, ~270 head-office roles cut, ~$110m targeted savings) is already showing traction — H1 FY26 operating profit up ~38% and net profit up from $11.8m to $15.7m year-on-year despite only modest sales growth

Units sold and foot-traffic conversion trends have improved (units +4.6% FY25, +2.6% Q1 FY26), suggesting the 'everyday low price' reset is winning back volume, which could translate into margin recovery once cost discipline and pricing stabilise
Warehouse Stationery remains a structurally higher-margin, growing segment (H1 FY26 sales +5.7%, Print & Copy Centre +7.2% FY25) that partially offsets weakness elsewhere in the portfolio

Dominant physical footprint (216 stores, 85% of NZ population within 20 minutes of a Warehouse store) and long-standing brand trust provide a scale/reach advantage that is difficult and costly for new entrants to replicate in a small market

Balance sheet retains meaningful liquidity headroom (~$207-354m undrawn facilities) and management has demonstrated willingness to curtail capex and working capital to protect cash flow through the downturn
bear_case: Group operating margin has been near breakeven for three consecutive years (FY23 2.6%, FY24 1.9%, FY25 1.3% on operating-profit-to-sales pre-IFRS16 basis), leaving very little cushion against further competitive or macro shocks

Structural margin pressure from an intentional low-price strategy amid intense competition (Kmart, Briscoes, Bunnings, cross-border online) may persist regardless of cost cuts, capping the ceiling on any earnings recovery

Heavy reliance on NZ consumer discretionary spending, which management itself describes as subdued with no clear catalyst for recovery, directly exposes apparel, home and Noel Leeming's big-ticket categories to continued softness

Large, largely fixed lease liability base (~$709m) and associated interest/principal cash outflows constrain financial flexibility and cannot be quickly reduced even if trading conditions deteriorate further

Leadership/strategic instability — three CEOs in under two years (permanent CEO departure, Interim CEO John Journee, now Mark Stirton) plus a wholesale executive team refresh — creates execution risk just as the turnaround plan is being implemented, and the FY25 annual report itself flags 'Leadership' and 'Culture' as top enterprise risks

No dividend and a nearly halved equity base since FY18 (from $479m to ~$300-310m) reflect a multi-year value destruction that has not yet clearly reversed; TheMarket.com's 2024 closure after five years underscores a track record of costly, unsuccessful strategic initiatives
